newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MANDELA STAYS ON SHIP IN FRESH BID FOR ZAIRE TALKS.
newsitem.headline: MANDELA STAYS ON SHIP IN FRESH BID FOR ZAIRE TALKS.

text.p: South Africa's Nelson Mandela made fresh efforts on Saturday to bring Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila together at sea and head off a bloody battle for Kinshasa.

With Kabila's rebels mustering men and materials and building up for a final push on Zaire's capital, Mandela remained on board the converted icebreaker SAS Outeniqua in Congo's port of Pointe Noire for Mobutu to join him.

Kabila, who failed to show for talks on Friday citing security concerns, left Angola's capital Luanda by plane on Saturday and a senior Western diplomat said he was apparently on his way to the seaborne summit.
"We believe Kabila has left Luanda and is on his way to meet Mobutu," the diplomat told Reuters.

South African officials said Mandela and Mohamed Sahnoun, the U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy on Zaire, held talks early on Saturday before Sahnoun left the Outeniqua and went into Pointe Noire where the ship was moored.

One said Sahnoun had most likely gone into town to see Mobutu, who stayed the night on shore with Congo's president, Pascal Lissouba, after Kabila failed to show for a rendezvous in international waters off Angola.
Kabila, who remained in Angola's capital Luanda, criticised security concerns and negotiating arrangements.

"I will go to the ship tomorrow if I receive adequate assurances from the South Africans tomorrow that security arrangements are in place," he told a news conference in Angola's capital Luanda on Friday.
"If we wanted to we could win this militarily in two weeks. Suggestions that I am stalling for time are ridiculous. I am interested in finding a peaceful solution to the problem."

South African officials said security on the Outeniqua would be tightened to meet Kabila's concerns, with particular attention to Mobutu's bodyguards, and that they expected the talks to go ahead on Saturday.
"We expect a repetition of what was due to happen to take place today but we don't know when," Pieter Swanepoel, South African foreign ministry spokesman, told reporters on the ship.
"We let people on board yesterday who obviously weren't journalists but were posing as journalists," Swanepoel said.
"We asked people for press credentials but they did not all have press credentials. Because they were accompanying the president (Mobutu), we let them on board," he added.
Mobutu boarded the Russian-built Outeniqua in Pointe Noire with great difficulty on Friday. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a make-shift ramp.
Aged 66 and suffering from prostate cancer, he is one of Africa's most enduring strongmen, backed during the Cold War by the United States as a bulwark against Soviet communism.
He has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but his illness and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on the former Belgian colony.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October and now control around three quarters of Zaire, mustered in force at Kikwit and pressed on with their march on the capital.
Mobutu aides say talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.

Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must go and has refused to declare a truce for the talks. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
